handbookNote: CLASSIFICATION: Vermont is a REAL-EXAM notary state, unlike most states in the 2026-08 batch which are application-only. 26 V.S.A. Section 5341(b)(5) requires a non-attorney initial applicant to 'pass a basic examination approved by the Office based on the statutes, rules, and ethics relevant to notarial acts' before a commission issues. This is corroborated two ways: (1) Section 5305(b)(1)(A) expressly exempts Vermont-licensed attorneys in good standing from 'the examination requirement set forth in subsection 5341(b)' -- an exemption that would make no sense if there were no exam to exempt them from; and (2) the Secretary of State's own Notary FAQ states plainly that 'Initial applicants submitting an application on or after February 1, 2021 will need to pass an examination based on the statutes, rules, and ethics relevant to notarial acts.' The Administrative Rules for Notaries Public (effective February 26, 2025), Part 4-2(e), restates the same requirement in rule form. STATUTE: 26 V.S.A. Chapter 103, the Uniform Law on Notarial Acts (Vermont's 2019 RULONA enactment, effective July 1, 2019) -- 34 operative sections spanning Sections 5301-5305 (general provisions, definitions, exemptions), 5321-5324 (Office duties, advisor appointees, rulemaking, fees), 5341-5345 (commissioning/qualifications/exam, discipline grounds, renewal/CE, database, prohibitions/offenses), and 5361-5380 (notarial-act authority, certificate/stamp requirements, interstate/tribal/federal/foreign recognition, and remote/electronic notarization). Full text fetched directly from legislature.vermont.gov section-by-section (curl with a browser User-Agent, since both legislature.vermont.gov and sos.vermont.gov returned errors to default WebFetch/curl requests) and compiled to temp/handbooks/vt/notary.txt. This was supplemented with the Office of Professional Regulation's Administrative Rules for Notaries Public (eff. Feb 26, 2025, 23 pages, fetched as a PDF from outside.vermont.gov) -- the current implementing rule, which supplies substantial additional testable detail beyond the bare statute text (exam/exemption mechanics, physical and electronic stamp requirements, Special Endorsement eligibility, remote-notarization identity-proofing quiz specifications, continuing-education course rules, and OPR complaint/contested-case procedure). REAL EXAM MECHANICS (Step 2 finding): the actual item count and passing score are NOT PUBLISHED anywhere. Checked and confirmed absent from: (1) the SOS Notary FAQ page (sos.vermont.gov/notaries-public/notary-faqs), which only restates the statutory 'based on the statutes, rules, and ethics' language with no numbers; (2) OPR's 2020 notary commission information letter (a primary-source PDF), which states only that 'further information about the examination will be available early next year' with no follow-up numeric detail ever published on the SOS site; (3) the Administrative Rules for Notaries Public (Feb 2025) themselves, which restate the same qualitative standard with zero mention of item count, passing score, time limit, or format; and (4) the National Notary Association's Vermont page (nationalnotary.org, checked Nov 2025 update), whose own how-to-become-a-notary checklist says only 'Pass the exam' with identical qualitative language and no numbers. Unlike states such as Pennsylvania (Pearson VUE, passing scaled score of 75) or California (PSI, scored exam with a published passing threshold), Vermont's exam is NOT vendor-administered -- OPR's own FAQ confirms 'Your notary commission is not linked to any outside association, vendor or company,' and the application FAQ describes the exam as embedded directly in the online licensing application itself ('You will be asked to answer questions within the application'), not a separately scheduled, proctored test. Given genuine, repeated, good-faith research across every source category this project's exam-mechanics audit checks, this is reported as confirmed 'not published' rather than left ambiguous or guessed. CONTENT DEPTH: real and substantial -- 34 statute sections plus a 23-page current administrative rules document supported 228 grounded raw questions across six topic buckets (definitions/general provisions; commissioning/qualifications/exam; notarial acts/authority/certificates; interstate-federal-foreign recognition; remote/electronic notarization; administrative procedures/continuing education) before deduplication -- comfortably within this project's established 200-250 question floor for exam-tier notary states, with no filler, invented facts, or restated duplicate questions used to reach that range. ELECTRONIC-NOTARIZATION ENDORSEMENT QUIRK: a base Vermont commission does NOT by itself authorize notarial acts on electronic records or for remotely located individuals (Section 5341(e)) -- a notary must separately apply for and pay a second $30 fee for a 'Special Endorsement' (Section 5324(b), Section 5341(d)) layered on top of the base $30 commission fee. A further quirk: Vermont notaries may certify copies ONLY of a tangible copy of an ELECTRONIC record (Section 5362(c); Administrative Rules Part 5-1(b) explicitly bars certifying 'any other forms of records') -- meaning, unusually, a Vermont notary cannot certify a plain photocopy of a paper original the way notaries in many other states can. The physical official stamp may NOT include the Vermont State Seal (Administrative Rules Part 5-3(b)(iii)(A)), and the statute's 10-year default audiovisual-recording retention period for remote acts (Section 5379(k)) has been shortened to 7 years by the current administrative rule (Part 8-2(f)), which the statute itself expressly permits by rule. PRICING: $9.99 (999 cents), matching this project's established real-exam notary tier (the same tier used for Colorado, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Ohio, Illinois, and other genuine-exam states) rather than the discounted $0.50/$0.75/$0.99 tiers reserved for the application-only batch -- because Vermont, unlike most of the August 2026 batch, has a real, currently-enforced statutory examination requirement under Section 5341(b)(5), even though its specific item count and passing score are not publicly disclosed.
